title: Update on review by blast radius: Anthropic publishes the tiered review policy behind Claude Code, where the share of PRs reverted fell over 40% as merged PRs doubled
summary:
The Claude Code team at Anthropic has published how it reviews code now that Claude writes about 90% of the product's code. Review was not removed, but most of the reading moved to machines. The stated goal is that most pull requests merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents, and that total human time on review and on fixing what bad code breaks goes down. Between June and September, merged pull requests on Claude Code more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40%. Separately, across Anthropic's monorepo (not only Claude Code), changes per day rose from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September.

What is new since this site's 2026-09-14 item on risk-tiered review is the full policy. A classifier sets each change's risk tier from the change itself, not from who wrote it. Low-risk changes such as docs and flagged additive features merge with no human approval once automated and security checks pass. Ordinary changes need one person, and the highest-risk code and a small set of paths need two. Some paths, including any CI workflow file, always need a person. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths, and an agent's approval never counts as a person's. The person who prompted an agent-written change counts as a required reviewer. Past incidents and reverts are collected into an expert-checked set of cases that the AI reviewer is scored against daily, and each new incident adds a case.

The account comes from the vendor of the tool being reviewed, describing its own team.
observer: Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt and Qing Wang of Anthropic, describing the review process of the team that builds Claude Code and reporting that team's own revert and pull-request figures
leadTimeEstimate: ~6-12 months before risk-tiered, partly human-free approval is written into enterprise review policy
whyItMatters: **Risk sets the review, not authorship** — a classifier decides how many humans approve a change, so review effort tracks blast radius rather than volume.
**Accountability is assigned explicitly** — the person who prompted an agent must approve its change, and agent approvals never count as human ones.
**Review quality gets a feedback loop** — adding incidents and reverts to an eval the reviewer is scored against daily makes the reviewer something the team measures and maintains.
recommendedActions: **Write down your risk tiers** — list which paths always need a human and which change types could merge on green checks, before review load forces it.
**Name the prompter as reviewer** — make the engineer who directed an agent a required approver, so ownership of agent-written code is never ambiguous.
risksAndCaveats: **Vendor describing its own tool** — Anthropic makes both Claude Code and the AI review it describes, and the figures have not been independently checked.
**Favourable conditions** — a team building an AI coding tool, with heavy CI and staged releases, may tolerate human-free merges more easily than most.
